title: Nominet DRS D00029109 (immersiveexperiences.co.uk) — Immerssive Experiences v Mr Mario Di Maggio
text:

D00029109

Immersive Dome Experiences Ltd

4. Factual Background
The Complainant is a company registered in the UK since January 2017. One of the
directors of the Complainant is the owner of UK trade mark number UK00003392335
for a stylised version of the expression “Immersive Experiences” shown below (the
“Trade Mark”). The Trade Mark has a filing date of 15 April 2019 and a registration
date of 16 August 2019.
The Trade Mark is registered in respect of a wide range of goods and services,
including “provision of exhibitions for entertainment purposes” and “entertainment
services”.
The Complainant has provided a broad description of its trading activities in relation
to the provision of immersive dome experiences, mobile planetariums, and
educational workshops across the UK. However, no evidence of its trading activity
(such as advertising, social media following, invoices, company accounts, turnover
data, third party media coverage, public reviews, etc.) has been provided, save for a
link to its website at <immersive-experiences.co.uk> where it is clear that the
Complainant trades under the name “Immersive Experiences”.
The Respondent is an individual who operates a business trading under the name
"Immersive Theatres 360° Experiences", operating from the domain name
<immersive-theatres.com>. The Respondent’s business appears to be very similar (if
not identical) to that of the Complainant, being the provision of portable inflatable
2

domes within which an audio-visual educational or entertainment “experience” is
projected for the benefit of an audience within the dome.
5. Parties’ Contentions
The Complainant asserts that, as the owner of the Trade Mark, they have exclusive
rights to use that brand and prevent any confusingly similar brands from being used
by third parties in connection with activities similar to those covered by the Trade
Mark.
The Complainant also asserts that they have developed unregistered rights
protected by the law of passing off as a result of their trading in the “immersive
experiences sector” in the last decade. Their position is that the relevant public
associate the name “Immersive Experiences” with the Complainant.
The Complainant’s position is that the Domain Name constitutes an Abusive
Registration because it targets the Complainant’s established brand, creates
confusion in the marketplace, diverts customers, and disrupts the Complainant’s
business operations. The Complainant also contends that the registration and use of
the Domain Name is an attempt to “free ride” on the Complainant’s reputation in
bad faith.
The Respondent submits that the use of the expression “Immersive Experiences” as
part of the Domain Name is descriptive since the Respondent’s business is the
provision of “immersive experiences”.
The Complainant submitted a Reply which reads as correspondence directed
towards the Respondent rather than submissions filed for consideration by the
Expert. The Reply has not been taken into account for the purposes of this decision
(although it is noted that the content of the Reply would not have affected the
outcome of this decision in any event).
6. Discussions and Findings
Under paragraph 2.2 of the Policy, the Complainant must prove, on the balance of
probabilities, each of the two elements set out in paragraphs 2.1.1 and 2.1.2 of the
Policy, namely that the Complainant has Rights in respect of a name or mark which is
identical or similar to the Domain Name; and that the Domain Name, in the hands of
the Respondent, is an Abusive Registration.
Rights
Paragraph 1 of the Policy provides that Rights means “rights enforceable by the
Complainant, whether under English law or otherwise, and may include rights in
descriptive terms which have acquired a secondary meaning”.
3

The requirement to demonstrate Rights under the Policy does not have a high
threshold. Rights may be established by way of a trade mark registration, or
unregistered rights arising from use of a name to the standard required under
common law.
The Complainant has provided details of the Trade Mark. The text of that trade mark
registration is identical with the text of the Domain Name. The goods and services
covered by the Trade Mark are the same as those provided by both the Complainant
and the Respondent.
This is sufficient to establish Rights for the purposes of the present complaint.
It is noted that the Trade Mark is registered in the name of “Zeeshaan Dinally” rather
than the Complainant. Zeeshaan Dinally is one of the directors of the Complainant
and shares the same contact address as the Complainant on the UK IPO records, and
the Expert is therefore content to find that the Complainant is an authorised user of
the Trade Mark for the purposes of this Complaint.
The Domain Name comprises the name “immersiveexperiences” and the top-level
domain suffix “.co.uk”, which may be disregarded for the purpose of comparison.
The text component of the Trade Mark is plainly identical with the text of the
Domain Name.
The Complainant has made extensive reference to the nature and extent of its
trading activity but has provided no evidence (save as referred to in the following
paragraph) beyond mere assertions, and the Expert attaches no weight to that part
of the Complaint.
The Complainant has demonstrated a level of trading activity through its registration
and use of the domain <immersive-experiences.co.uk>. It is clear that this is highly
similar to the Domain Name, differing only in the presence of a hyphen. The Expert
finds that the Complainant has at least a de minimis level of Rights associated with
the registration and use of its domain name, to which the Domain Name is highly
similar.
The Expert finds that the Complainant has Rights in respect of a name or mark which
is identical with or highly similar to the Domain Name.
Abusive Registration
Paragraph 1 of the Policy defines “Abusive Registration” as a domain name which
either:
i. was registered or otherwise acquired in a manner which, at the time when
the registration or acquisition took place, took unfair advantage of or was
unfairly detrimental to the Complainant's Rights; or
4

ii. is being or has been used in a manner which has taken unfair advantage of
or has been unfairly detrimental to the Complainant's Rights;
This general definition is supplemented by paragraph 5.1 of the Policy which
provides a non-exhaustive list of factors which may be evidence that the Domain
Name is an Abusive Registration. Paragraph 8.1 of the Policy provides a similar non-
exhaustive list of factors which may be evidence that the Domain Name is not an
Abusive Registration.
The Policy requires the Complainant to prove, on the balance of probabilities, that
the Domain Name is an Abusive Registration. The burden of proof is therefore firmly
on the Complainant.
The Complainant’s case is that the Respondent purposely registered the Domain
Name in the knowledge of the Complainant’s Rights for the purposes of unfairly
disrupting the Complainant’s business within the meaning of paragraph 5.1.1.3 of
the Policy, and to confuse people into thinking that the Domain Name is connected
with the Complainant under paragraph 5.1.2 of the Policy.
The Complainant has claimed to have a national footprint across the United
Kingdom, and established online presence and high online search visibility. In the
absence of supporting evidence, no finding is made on this basis.
The Complainant has also suggested that the registration and use of the Domain
name is leading to loss of enquiries and bookings, creating customer confusion, and
driving increased marketing costs to counteract confusion. Again, no evidence has
been provided of this.
The Respondent’s case is that the use oft the Domain Name
<immersiveexperienes.co.uk> is a legitimate description of their business of
providing “immersive experiences”. In other words, the Respondent seeks to rely on
paragraph 8.1.2 of the Policy in that the Domain Name is generic or descriptive and
the Respondent is making fair use of it, and therefore does not constitute an Abusive
Registration.
By their own admission, the Respondent trades under the name "Immersive
Theatres 360° Experiences" or just “Immersive Theatres” and operates from the
domain name <immersive-theatres.com>. The content of the site hosted at the
Domain Name appears to be nearly identical to that hosted on <immersive-
theatres.com>.
This leads to the question of why the Respondent, as the owner of a business
operating under the name “Immersive Theatres”, has chosen to register the Domain
Name <immersiveexperiences.co.uk> to create a mirror of its website.
Given the similarity of the names between the respective businesses of the
Complainant and the Respondent through the mutual adoption of the word
5

“Immersive”, it appears to be a strange choice on the part of the Respondent to
actively choose a domain name that (a) is different to its own trading name, and (b)
adopts the same name as a competitor in the market.
It is inconceivable that the Respondent would not have been aware of the
Complainant, either as a result of operating in the same sector, or from online
searches of the name “Immersive Experiences” prior to registration of the Domain
Name. In any event, the Response does not state that the Respondent was unaware
of the Complainant’s activities, and the Respondent does not appear to have
changed their activities in the light of the complaint and the surrounding
circumstances.
The only reasonable conclusion is that the Respondent purposely chose to register
and use the Domain Name for the purposes of unfairly disrupting the Complainant’s
business within the meaning of paragraph 5.1.1.3. The Respondent has their own
separate website at <immersive-theatres.com> and yet chose to replicate it under a
name already adopted by a competitor.
Given the Complainant’s existing Rights (and long-standing use of the domain name
<immersive-experiences.co.uk>), it is reasonable to infer that an average internet
user would assume that the Domain Name is somehow affiliated with, authorised by,
or otherwise connected to the Complainant, when that is not the case.
Customers attempting to locate the Complainant’s online presence may be diverted
to the Respondent, and given the mutual use of “Immersive” in the names and the
seemingly identical business offerings, there is clearly a risk that those customers
may be confused and may end up purchasing services from the Respondent instead
of from the Complainant. Paragraph 5.1.2 of the Policy does not require actual
confusion to be proven, but just that confusion be likely, and the Expert finds this to
be the case.
This is due to the strong similarity of the names adopted by each party, their highly
similar business offerings, the Complainant’s existing domain name, the fact that the
Respondent already has their own separate trading presence online, and the
absence of any credible reason for adopting the Domain Name having been provided
by the Respondent.
The Respondent’s submissions that the name “immersive experiences” is generic or
descriptive are noted, but are not considered sufficiently persuasive to displace the
clear inference that the use of the Domain Name by the Respondent presents a real
risk of confusion. This submission may have carried more weight if the Respondent
were actually to have been separately trading under the name “Immersive
Experiences”, but since that is not the case, and the Respondent operates under a
similar name, the finding of an Abusive Registration on the grounds that the
Respondent, on balance of probabilities, adopted the Domain Name to disrupt or
associate with the Complainant is maintained.
6

There appears to be a wider history of the dispute between the parties and the DRS
is not the forum for resolution of that dispute. For the avoidance of doubt for both
parties, this decision is made purely on the basis of the submissions of each party
and is limited in scope to whether the registration and use of the Domain Name
constitutes an Abusive Registration. No finding is made in relation to the validity or
enforceability of the Trade Mark, infringement of the Trade Mark, or in relation to
any claims for passing off, unfair competition, or reputational damage.
7. Decision
The Expert finds that the Complainant has proved that it has Rights in a name which
is highly similar to the Domain Name and that the Domain Name, in the hands of the
Respondent, is an Abusive Registration. The Expert therefore directs that the Domain
Name be transferred to the Complainant.
Signed Dated 26 May 2026
Simon Sellars
